parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> BikeFix is a mobile bicycle repair service in a large city. Demand is higher in spring and summer. The owner wants to buy an electric van to reach more customers at weekends. BikeFix currently advertises with leaflets and social media. The owner is considering dynamic pricing (higher prices at peak times). Two finance options are being considered: a bank loan or leasing the van.
> 
> **Table 2.1 – Extract from BikeFix cash flow forecast (first quarter) \$s**
> 
> |   | **January** | **February** | **March** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Opening balance | 2 000 | 3 500 | 2 800 |
> | Cash inflows (sales) | 6 000 | 5 400 | 7 200 |
> | Cash outflows (wages, fuel, parts, ads) | 4 500 | 6 100 | 5 900 |
> | **Net cash flow** | **1 500** | **X** | **1 300** |
> | **Closing balance** | **3 500** | 2 800 | **Y** |

Which source of finance is likely to be better for BikeFix to buy the electric van?

- Bank loan
- Leasing

Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
With leasing there is a lower initial cash outlay **[K]**, which means BikeFix can keep cash for parts and advertising **[Ap]**, reducing liquidity risk while testing weekend demand before committing to an asset for the long term **[An]**. However, BikeFix would never own the van and there may be limits on mileage and how the van can be modified to carry, for example, tools **[Ap]**

With a loan, ownership of the asset appears on the balance sheet** [K]**, increasing the value of the business, and allows for long-term use without mileage limits **[Ap]**. As a result, total cost may be lower over the van’s life, improving profitability once demand is proven** [An]**

Overall, though, because demand is seasonal and still growing, leasing is better now to protect cash flow and match payments to use** [E]**. BikeFix can switch to ownership later when revenue is more stable** **and when the cost of purchasing could well be lower **[E] **

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Award up to 2 marks for each of the following:
> 
>   - State two valid points relevant to the question, each with a different viewpoint → 2 K marks
>   - Apply each point clearly to the stimulus → 2 Ap marks
>   - Develop each point → 2 An marks
>   - Make a justified decision → 2 E marks
> - **Points might include**
> 
>   - Leasing – why it may be better
>   
>     - Low upfront payment keeps cash for parts/ads in seasonal business
>     - Maintenance often included and it may be easier to upgrade as technology improves
>     - Matches payments to usage; useful while testing weekend demand
>   - Loan (ownership) – why it may be better
>   
>     - Asset owned; no mileage/condition penalties; resale value at the end
>     - Total cost may be lower long-term if utilisation is high and rates are reasonable
>   - Judgement
>   
>     - Current cash balance and forecast (quiet winter vs busy summer)
>     - Interest rate offered vs lease terms; creditworthiness.
>     - Expected mileage/usage intensity; reliability of demand from dynamic pricing

parts.problem_md: **Define **'government grant'
parts.solution_md:
Money given by the government that does not have to be repaid **[K] **when the business receiving it meets set criteria, such as creating jobs **[K]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure that you do not confuse grants with government loans, which do have to be repaid, often at a low rate of interest

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**Safari Adventures (SA) **

Tokumbo is a sole trader. He started SA 2 years ago in country X. Tokumbo had previously worked for a company selling holidays. SA organises safari tours which take tourists to view wild animals on a game reserve. Most of SA’s customers are tourists from other countries. Tokumbo did not have any objectives when he started SA but knows they are important for his business.

SA uses its own vehicles for the 7 day safari tours and provides accommodation in small local hotels. Tokumbo employs 4 safari guides, 1 for each of the 4 vehicles. The safari guides drive the tourists around the game reserve. There is 1 additional employee who helps Tokumbo in the office with administration. Tokumbo thinks SA needs a website so tourists can book directly with them rather than booking through holiday companies that charge SA a fee.

Tokumbo is considering the following three options for the future growth of SA safari tours:

- Option 1 - increasing the number of safari guides and vehicles to increase the number of customers from the existing target market
- Option 2 – targeting young people who want to camp and sleep in a tent on their safari
- Option 3 - targeting high-income tourists who prefer to stay in luxury hotels

Information about these three options is outlined in Appendix 3.

Tokumbo plans to provide more training for his employees whichever option he chooses. He wants his existing employees to have a wider knowledge of the wild animals on the game reserve and to be able to provide high-quality customer service. Tokumbo has to decide which method of training to use.

**Appendix 1 **

**Newspaper article in Main News, September 2022 **

**Tourism takes off**

Country X is becoming a popular holiday destination for tourists from other countries.

There is an increased demand from high-income tourists who want to stay in luxury hotels whilst on safari tours. These tourists are willing to pay high prices. There is also a new trend for younger people who want cheaper holidays. They prefer to camp and sleep in tents on game reserves rather than stay in hotels.

Are the many safari businesses in country X ready to target these new markets?

The use of e-commerce to find and book safari tours by tourists from other countries is offering both opportunities and threats to businesses in country X.

The inflation rate in country X has increased to 4% which may affect some of our local safari businesses.

**Appendix 2 **

**Email from Tokumbo’s accountant**

To: Tokumbo

From: Accountant

Subject: Source of finance for the new vehicles

New vehicles will be needed whichever option you choose for the future growth of your business.

I have considered several sources of finance you could use for the new vehicles. Interest rates on bank loans have fallen to 2% whilst interest rates on savings are 3%. I think you should choose from one of the following sources:

- Leasing
- Bank loan
- Retained profit

We can meet to discuss these sources if that would help you to decide.

**Appendix 3 **

**SA’s three options for a 7 day safari tour**

|   | Option 1 More existing safari tours | Option 2 Camping safari tours | Option 3 Luxury safari tours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forecast number of tourists per week | 16 | 32 | 10 |
| Total costs per week for SA to provide these safari tours | \$12 000 | \$8000 | \$20 000 |
| Average cost per tourist | \$750 | ? | ? |
| Price per tourist | \$1000 | \$400 | \$2400 |

Consider the following **three** sources of finance Tokumbo could use for the new vehicles:

- Leasing
- Bank loan
- Retained profit

Which source should he choose? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2022-paper-21-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Leasing allows SA to use the safari vehicles without requiring a large upfront payment because costs are spread over time. This helps manage cash flow **[An]**, which is an important consideration for a small business like SA **[Ap]. **Additionally, leasing makes it easier to upgrade vehicles regularly, ensuring SA always has modern, reliable transport for safari tours **[An]**

A bank loan could provide the necessary funds, but it would require repayment with interest, adding to SA's costs **[An]**. Given that interest rates are 2% **[Ap]**, this might seem attractive. However, as a sole trader, Tokumbo would be personally liable for the loan, putting his assets at risk if SA struggled to make repayments **[An]**

Retained profit, if available, would be the cheapest option. However, SA has only been operating for 2 years **[Ap]**, so it is unlikely to have accumulated enough retained profit to purchase the vehicles outright **[An]**. Additionally, using all available retained profit could leave SA without reserves for emergencies  **[An]**

Leasing offers the most flexible and low-risk option **[E]** for SA to acquire new vehicles, supporting its growth plans without overstretching its financial resources **[E]**. Although SA will never own the vehicles, it will be able to use them to provide safari tours, and there is less personal risk for sole trader Tokumbo **[Ap]** if the business fails **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Leasing**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Allows SA to use vehicles without large upfront capital → preserves cash flow
>     - Monthly payments spread cost → easier management of cash flow
>     - Lease company covers maintenance → lower repair expenses
>     - Option to buy at lease end → potential asset ownership
>     - Easier to refresh fleet regularly → access to new models
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Total lease cost often exceeds purchase price → higher long-term expense
>     - SA does not own the vehicle → must return at lease end → risk of service gaps
>     - Break in replacement → safari tours may be cancelled
> - **Bank loan**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Receive full \$20 000 in one transaction → immediate capital for vehicles
>     - Usually quick to arrange → fast access to funds
>     - Repayable over several years at ~2 % → lower monthly instalments
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Interest payments add to financing cost → increases total expense
>     - As a small sole trader → likely higher interest rate → heavier burden
>     - Personal assets at risk if defaulted → requires security or guarantee
>     - Must prepare business plan and documents → extra time and effort
> - **Retained profit**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - No repayment or interest → cheapest finance option
>     - No collateral needed → no personal asset risk
>     - Avoids bank interest → reduces overall cost
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - SA only two years old → may lack sufficient retained earnings
>     - Drains reserves → no cushion for emergencies
>     - Reduces owner’s draw → less profit distribution
>     - Opportunity cost of 3 % savings interest lost
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Leasing spreads payments and covers maintenance → ideal if cash is tight and asset use is critical
>   - Bank loan provides full ownership and steady instalments → best if SA can secure favorable terms and afford interest
>   - Retained profit is cheapest but may not be available → suitable if reserves exist without compromising liquidity

**Extract:** **Playsafe Playground Equipment (PPE)** Kaari has always been creative and made wooden toys for her two children when they were young. Her children are now at school, so Kaari decided to start her own business making wooden playground equipment. Kaari started PPE as a sole trader business three years ago in country Z. She wants an income from the business but also wants to spend time with her children. Kaari wants the business to remain small. However, if the business grows Kaari may need to change to another type of business organisation. Kaari carries out all the management roles in the business. Kaari uses job production to produce high quality, individually designed playground equipment. Kaari designs all the equipment herself and she employs 3 skilled workers to help her make the products. PPE currently makes both large and small items of playground equipment each week. Kaari uses cost-plus pricing as every item of playground equipment uses different quantities of raw materials. She sells small items of playground equipment to retailers and large items of playground equipment to the Government. There are many competitors in this market. Kaari plans to obtain new machinery which will cost \$20 000. She is considering using crowd-funding as this is one way to raise capital for new business investment. Other options include leasing the machinery or asking the bank for a loan. Kaari has developed a new unique product this year. There are no other similar products in the market. **Appendix 1** **Advertisement for PPE** Buy your playground equipment from us. At PPE we manufacture high quality playground equipment and have better designs than our competitors. All our equipment has been fully tested and is guaranteed to meet legal safety standards. We are the main supplier of playground equipment to the Government for public parks - so you know our equipment can be trusted! Contact us today for a price list. **Appendix 2** **Cost and revenue information for PPE in 2021** | | **Small item of playground**

**equipment** | **Large item of playground**

**equipment** | |---|---|---| | Average selling price | \$100 | \$1 000 | | Average cost of manufacture | \$25 | \$500 | | Output each week | 15 | 3 | **Appendix 3** **Newspaper article – Main News 1st October 2021** **Children need to get more exercise and play outside** Research suggests that playing outside helps children relax after school and improves their health. The Government in country Z has allocated \$10m to spend on improving children’s playgrounds in public places. This means there will be \$5 000 to spend on equipment for each public playground. Retailers have reported increasing demand for small items of playground equipment as parents want to have these products at home. This trend is expected to continue. Consider the advantages and disadvantages to PPE of using the following **three** sources of finance to obtain new machinery: - Crowd-funding - Bank loan - Leasing Which source should PPE choose? **Justify **your answer. Refer to the following[ insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2021-paper-2-case-study-v2---new.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Crowd-funding could test public reaction to Kaari's unique new playground equipment designs **[Ap]**, potentially attracting retailers and government customers. However, if PPE doesn't reach the \$20,000 goal **[Ap]**, all money must be returned. There's also a risk of competitors stealing ideas in this competitive market **[An]**

A bank loan would provide the full \$20,000 upfront, allowing immediate machinery purchase. PPE could repay over years as revenue increases from both large and small equipment production **[Ap]**. However, as a small sole trader **[Ap]**, PPE may face high interest rates, and Kaari might need to provide collateral, risking personal assets **[An]**

Leasing avoids large upfront costs, helping cash flow for this 3-employee business **[Ap]**. The leasing company would handle maintenance, letting Kaari focus on design and production. However, it's potentially more expensive long-term, and PPE wouldn't own the equipment after the lease **[An]**

A bank loan seems most suitable for PPE **[E]**. It provides immediate access to machinery, increasing production capacity without exposing designs **[Ap]** to competitors **[E], **which may be the case with crowdfunding **[E]**. Unlike leasing, PPE would own the asset outright. To reduce her personal risks, Kaari could consider applying for government-backed loan schemes for better terms **[E]**

> - **Crowd-funding**

>   - **Advantages**
>

>   
>     - Interest payments over life of loan → increases overall financing cost
>     - Requires collateral or personal guarantee → higher risk for Kaari

> 
>   - **Advantages**

>

**Extract:**

**Cell Covers (CC) **

Aisha worked for several years for a company that repairs mobile (cell) phones in country Z. She had always wanted to be her own boss and decided to leave her job to set up CC to produce covers for mobile phones. She went into partnership with her brother, Aruna. He worked as an Operations Manager for a company producing children’s clothes.

The sources of finance for the business were \$10 000 of savings from each partner and a bank loan of \$10 000. CC was also given a government grant to help the new business get started. CC leased a factory, bought some equipment and had to pay some expenses before the business had regular cash inflows.

CC’s current product is a range of standardised phone covers which are sold in the mass market. These are sold using a competitive pricing method through mobile phone shops. CC employs 10 skilled production workers who are paid just above the legal minimum wage. These workers have been trained how to operate the equipment and work as a team on the production line. During the production process there is a lot of waste plastic produced and CC sends this to landfill sites. The business has just completed its second year of trading.

CC is about to launch a new range of individual personalised phone covers. It will need to recruit 2 additional production workers. Aruna knows that the marketing mix for this new product may have to be different to the marketing mix used for the standardised products. The new product will be aimed at a niche market of high income consumers between the ages of 18 to 25. There are few other competitors in this market at present.

**Appendix 1 **

**Newspaper article in Main News **

Country Z has been in a recession but the economy is now growing rapidly and unemployment is falling. With higher incomes the majority of people now own a mobile phone. This makes communication easier. Mobile banking is becoming more popular and it is used by a large percentage of the population.

**Appendix 2 **

**Advertisement for CC’s standardised mobile phone covers**

Do you want to protect your phone from damage? Then buy a phone cover from CC. Your phone will never be damaged if you use one of our high quality covers!!

We offer a range of standardised covers at competitive prices. The CC range has many different colours and designs so you will stand out from the crowd.

**Appendix 3 **

**Summary of CC’s financial information from the end of the second year of trading (\$)**

| Revenue | 800 000 |
|---|---|
| Cost of sales | 400 000 |
| Gross profit | 400 000 |
| Expenses | 250 000 |
| Profit | 150 000 |
| Current Assets | 20 000 |
| of which: Inventory | 5 000 |
| Current liabilities | 15 000 |

**Explain two** reasons why finance is needed by CC.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2020-paper-22-case-study-v2---new.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
CC needed finance to start up the business **[K]**. Aisha and Aruna needed \$30,000 initially, which came from \$10,000 of savings from each partner and a \$10,000 bank loan **[Ap]**. Start-up finance is required because CC had lots of costs to cover **[An]**, such as leasing a factory and buying production equipment, before they started making money **[An]**

Secondly, CC needs finance to expand **[K] **the business. CC is about to launch a new range of personalised phone covers. This will require hiring two more workers **[Ap]**. Expanding into new products costs money for things like developing the product, marketing it, and paying for extra staff **[An]**. Having finance allows CC to grow and take advantage of new opportunities in the phone cover market **[An]**

**Explain two** possible reasons why it might be difficult for ReBag to get a bank loan.

> **[case-study]**
> ReBag is a social enterprise. ReBag employs 30 people in four small towns in different parts of the country. They work from home and make a range of bags from pieces of old fabric (cloth).
> 
> Asha started the business three years ago using micro-finance. Last year ReBag’s revenue was \$700. Asha said: ‘Our external stakeholders want ReBag to employ people in five more towns. Getting a bank loan to expand the business will be a problem. What will I do about management? How will I inform workers about possible expansion?’
parts.solution_md:
ReBag might struggle to get a bank loan because of its very low revenue **[K]**, only \$700 last year **[Ap]**. With such small earnings, ReBag may not be able to afford loan payments, making banks hesitant to lend to them **[An]**

Another reason is that ReBag lacks assets to use as security for a loan** [K]**. The workers make bags from home **[Ap]**, so there is no factory or equipment the bank could take if ReBag cannot repay. Without collateral, banks have no way to recover their money if the business fails. This is especially concerning given ReBag's plan for rapid expansion, which could be financially risky **[An]**

parts.problem_md: **Explain four** factors a business should consider when choosing which source of finance to use for expansion.
parts.solution_md:
The business's legal form **[K]** affects finance options. Companies can issue new shares to existing shareholders to raise money for growth, but sole traders cannot, limiting the amount they can raise **[An]**

The amount needed **[K]** is also important. Bank loans or selling shares may be better for large amounts, whilst smaller amounts may be obtained from owner's savings or overdrafts **[An]**

Existing borrowing **[K]** should be considered, If a business already has many loans, getting another may be hard or expensive. A factory with several bank loans might choose to sell some assets instead of borrowing more **[An]**

Control **[K]** is also an important consideration. Selling new shares to outsiders could mean original owners lose power to make decisions. A family-owned restaurant might prefer a bank loan to keep full control, even if it costs more **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - In your answer:
> 
>   - Give four valid reasons related to the question → 4 K marks
>   - For each reason, explain how or why it matters using a cause–effect link → 4 An marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Relevant answers might include:
> 
>   - Legal form of business – if the business is a company, then share issue is an option/if the business is unincorporated then owner’s savings may have to be used as it cannot issue shares to raise finance
>   - Amount required – as the finance is for expansion then a large amount is likely to be required so sources such as bank loans or share issue may be chosen
>   - Purpose – as the finance is needed for expansion it is likely to be a large amount and so should be able to be repaid over a long period to make the repayments manageable
>   - Existing loans – if the business already has a high number of bank loans, then this may not be an option due to the already high expenses of paying the interest on loans
>   - Control of the business – if the business is a company, then issuing additional shares may lead to the original shareholders losing control of the business so may need to decide which is more important, expansion or control
>   - Cost of finance – the interest rate charged on the borrowing
>   - Length of time needed to repay
>   - Size of business

> **[case-study]**
> Paolo wants to start up a business making cakes. He plans to sell all of his products to a wholesaler. Paolo knows the packaging for his products will be important. He has prepared some financial and sales data. An extract from this data is shown in Table 1.1. Paolo is considering using crowdfunding as a source of finance. He knows the business will also need working capital.
>

> | Average cost per cake | \$4 |

**Explain one** advantage and **one** disadvantage to Paolo’s business of using crowdfunding as a source of finance.
parts.solution_md:
Crowdfunding does not require paying interest **[K]**, which means Paolo will not have extra cash outflows for his new start-up. This is helpful because he will be able to keep more of the money he makes from selling cakes to the wholesaler **[Ap]**, providing Paolo with a financial reward for taking the risk in setting up his own business **[An]**

However, Paolo may not raise enough money **[K]** through crowdfunding to cover his start-up costs. If he does not reach the full target amount, he might have to repay everyone who contributed, leaving him without any funding at all. This could delay the launch of his cake business **[Ap]** and force him to look for other sources of finance to cover costs like packaging and ingredients **[An]**

parts.problem_md: Do you think owner’s savings are the most suitable source of finance for a start-up business? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Owner's savings do not need to be repaid with interest **[K]**, so are a cheap form of finance. Sales revenue is likely to be low initially, so costs need to be controlled carefully to avoid business failure. However, the owner may not have enough savings to fully fund a business start-up, especially if specialist equipment or expensive stock is needed** [An]**

Interest must be paid on a bank loan, increasing expenses** [K]**, but the full amount needed to start up the business immediately may be available, so the owner will not miss out on opportunities. A detailed business plan will be needed to convince a bank that money borrowed can be paid back **[An]**

As long as they have enough, owner's savings are the best way to fund a start-up **[E]**. Keeping costs low by avoiding interest costs will help it to survive, especially as it builds up sales. Bank loans are more suitable for growing businesses that have a convincing trading history to appeal to lenders such as banks **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Do you think it is better for a private limited company to use debt (e.g. a loan) or equity (issuing more shares) as a source of long-term finance? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Debt finance, such as a bank loan, means they would get all the money at once, which is helpful for big purchases **[K]**. Also, owners keep full control of the company as they do not have to sell any shares. However, they must pay interest on the loan, which increases costs and could cause cash flow problems if sales are low **[An]**

Issuing more shares (equity) means the company would not have to pay interest or repay the money **[K]**, which helps cash flow. They would, though, have to pay dividends to the new shareholders, leaving less profit to reinvest. Also, the current owners would lose some control over decision making by bringing in new shareholders **[An]**

I recommend using debt finance. Although interest must be paid, the owners keep full control of the company **[E]**. This is important for a private limited company that may want to make decisions quickly without consulting lots of shareholders **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Do you think the amount of money needed is the most important factor for a sole trader to consider when deciding on an appropriate source of finance? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The amount of money needed is important because they might not have sufficient savings themselves **[K]** so would need to borrow more. The amount affects which options are available. For example, larger sums may require long-term financing like bank loans, while smaller amounts could use short-term options like overdrafts** [An]**

However, the sole trader's unlimited liability **[K]** is another crucial factor to consider. This reduces the finance options available and makes the business riskier to lenders. Whatever amount is needed, finance is likely to be more expensive and harder to obtain for a sole trader **[An]**

Unlimited liability is probably the most important factor because it limits the sole trader's financing choices and increases costs, regardless of the amount needed **[E]**. While the amount of money impacts the specific option chosen, it does not have as much influence on the overall availability and terms of financing as the sole trader's legal structure does **[E]**

parts.problem_md: **Define **‘working capital’.
parts.solution_md:
Working capital is the amount of capital available **[K] **to a business to pay its day-to-day expenses **[K]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Don't confuse working capital with cash flow, which is the flow of money into and out of a business over a period of time

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Knowledge 2
> 
>   - Give a clearly-stated, valid definition to achieve both knowledge [K] marks
>   - 2 marks for a full definition, 1 mark for a partial definition
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Amount of capital available to a business to pay its day-to-day expenses/costs [2]
> 
>   - OR The capital needed to finance the day to day running expenses (and pay the short-term debts of the business) [2]
>   - OR Current assets – current liabilities [2]
> - Partial definition e.g. funds used to buy inventory [1]
